title: Unlock modern web capabilities in your AI coding workflows

segments.text: [MUSIC PLAYING]
PHILIP WALTON: Hey, everybody.
My name is Philip Walton.
And today I want to start off by showing you a screen recording
that I made of two different demos.
Both of these demos look and function identically.
Both have dropdown menus that smoothly animate in and out.
They're both fully keyboard accessible.
They both support light dismiss.
And they both work in Chrome, Firefox, and Safari.
These demos were both also generated using AI.
In fact, they were generated using the same coding
agent, the same model, and the same prompt.
The difference, though, is the version on the left was
generated using an agent in its standard, default,
out-of-the-box configuration.
And the version on the right was generated using the same agent,
but with one extra thing installed,
and I'll get to that later.
But there is one more big difference
between these two demos.
If I open up DevTools, and I zoom in here on the Network
panel, you can see that the version on the left
loads 172 kilobytes, most of which is JavaScript.
Whereas, the one on the right loads less than 3k,
and uses absolutely no JavaScript.
And to be clear, that's 172 kilobytes over the wire,
minified and gzipped, with all of the production optimizations
turned on.
And I didn't modify this code at all.
This is what the AI suggested.
Now, admittedly, this is a bit of a contrived example
because no app is just a settings menu and nothing else.
Once you add more features, you might need
to add some more JavaScript.
Still, I do think this raises an interesting question.
Why are AI coding agents recommending a solution that
requires almost 172 kilobytes of JavaScript
when the same exact solution can be built in a way that
requires no JavaScript at all and still works across browsers?
So if you were at any of the talks
earlier today, you heard a lot about this,
a lot about how amazing AI is.
And don't get me wrong, AI is amazing.
It truly blows my mind every single day.
But that is just one side of the story.
The truth is that, while AI has transformed the software
industry, and it has enabled us developers
to write code way faster than ever before, there
is another side to the story.
AI is definitely not perfect.
And if you, like me, follow a lot of well-known frontend
developers on social media, then you'll
know that many of these folks are definitely not
shy about pointing out just how not perfect
these AI coding agents are, especially when it
comes to writing HTML and CSS.
And, you know, these folks, they're not wrong.
There have been so many amazing developments
on the web over the past few years
and, yet, if you ask a coding agent
to go build something for you on the web,
it's most likely not going to reach for the latest web
platform features to do it, even if those features really
are the best tool for the job.
And this isn't all that surprising
if you consider that most of the training data used
by these models was written during a time when
most developers had to support legacy browsers like Internet
Explorer.
But regardless of the reason, the reality
is that, for frontend web development,
coding agents do tend to recommend legacy solutions even
when there are better, more modern alternatives.
Another big problem we see with AI models
is that they have a knowledge gap.
Every model has a knowledge cutoff date
where any new developments on the web that
occurred after that date are just not included
in the model's training.
In the past year alone, Chrome has shipped more than 50 brand
new web features.
But due to these knowledge cutoffs, many of these features
are just completely unknown to these models.
And while techniques like RAG and web search
can help with this problem, they don't eliminate it entirely.
And if you ask a coding agent to use a feature that it's never
heard of, it'll usually do a web search.
But if you ask it to do something
that it thinks it already knows how to do,
then it'll often just reply confidently
right away without checking for more up-to-date information.
For example, here's some code that an agent generated
after I asked it to build a tooltip using the new interest
invokers API.
Now, if you look closely at the highlighted line of code,
you can see that the model used the interesttarget attribute,
which is not correct.
interesttarget was the attribute name when this API was first
proposed back in 2023.
But right before the API shipped in Chrome last fall,
the name was changed to interestfor.
And so that means that the code you see on the screen
will silently fail when run in a browser, which will
make it pretty hard to debug.
Now, this specific problem is probably
going to be fixed for this API in the next generation
of the models.
But the larger problem is not going away anytime soon.
A third problem we see is how AI models
make cross-browser support decisions.
In our testing, AI is way more conservative
than it needs to be when it comes to cross-browser support.
It's understandable that these models or these tool makers
would want to optimize for broad compatibility.
But now that we have initiatives like Baseline, which
includes compatibility data for nearly every web feature,
there's really no excuse for not using it.
Agents should not be making generic,
one-size-fits-all browser support recommendations.
They should be tailoring their recommendations
to the specific needs of your project.
So that's a quick overview of the main problems
we see with AI coding agents when it comes to modern web
development.
To recap, AI coding agents frequently
recommend legacy patterns, even though better, more modern
alternatives exist.
Second, AI models have blind spots and either aren't aware of
or have incorrect information about the latest web
platform features.
And third, AI models tend to make outdated,
one-size-fits-all browser support recommendations.
But the good news is that here, in Chrome, we
believe that these problems are all very solvable.
And we've been hard at work on a solution
that we're excited to share with you all today, an early preview.
We call it Modern Web Guidance.
Modern Web Guidance is a comprehensive and expert-vetted
set of skills covering all of Chrome's best practices
on building for the modern web.
This package embeds decades of Chrome's web platform experience
expertise directly into your coding agents.
And because it's based on skills,
it works with any AI coding platform.
You can install Modern Web Guidance
with this single command, npx modern-web-guidance install.
Or if you're using any of the IDEs
or coding agents shown here on the screen,
you can find and install Modern Web Guidance
directly from within these tools.
So I know, right now, the market is absolutely flooded
with new skills releases.
And as a developer, it can be challenging to keep up,
overwhelming even.
It's also especially hard to determine
which skills are good and worth using and which skills are--
let's face it-- basically just slop.
So I want to stress here that Modern Web Guidance is not
your ordinary skills pack.
This is something that we on the Chrome team
have been investing in a ton over the past six months.
And it's something that we're committed to investing in
for the long term.
So let's dive in and take a closer look at what's included
and how it works.
So Modern Web Guidance is comprised of two distinct levels
of guidance.
First, we have a set of high-level guides codifying
the best practices for broad web disciplines
like performance, accessibility, security,
user experience, and many more.
In addition to these high-level guides,
we also have a set of very specific low-level guides
covering web features that have been recently added
to the platform.
And we've seen that AI models just
don't yet have a good understanding of how
to use them properly.
All of these guides have been created by members of the Chrome
team, in collaboration with a number of external subject
matter experts that we've hired to contribute to this project.
And because these guides focus on core web platform features,
they will work regardless of whatever framework
or stack you're using, or anything like that.
Now, before I dig deeper into the specifics of these guides,
I want to give you all a quick overview of how
the tool works at a high level.
So when you're using a coding agent out of the box,
the flow is pretty simple.
The user types a prompt into the tool.
The prompt is given to the AI model, which then
produces an output response.
If you're using Modern Web Guidance,
then, before the AI produces an output,
it'll perform a semantic search locally
within the Modern Web Guidance package
to see if any of our guides match
the use case in the prompt.
If there are no matches, then those guides
will get added to the context window.
And if they're-- sorry.
If there are matches, those guys will add it
to the context window.
If there are no matches, the AI will respond as normal.
Now, note that this is a bit different from how
most skills work where each skill is
a distinct skill that MD file.
With Modern Web Guidance, we expose a single entry point
skill that has access to a CLI that does the search.
And we do this because we currently have
more than 100 distinct guides.
And we plan to add likely hundreds more.
So it just doesn't scale to expose these all as single,
top-level skilled MD files.
So let's take a closer look at what these guides look like.
Now, I mentioned before that we have both high-level discipline
skills and low-level feature guides.
The high-level guides are very similar to the skills
that you've probably seen before.
But for the low-level feature guides,
we took a different approach that I think is pretty novel,
and so I want to talk about it.
First, rather than focusing on the features themselves
and documenting how those features work,
instead, each of these guides focuses on a distinct use case
that one of these features unlocks
or makes easier to implement.
For example, one of the use cases that we identified
for the View Transitions API that's been unlocked was
"Visually connect persisting elements across different page
states or navigations by smoothly morphing their size,
position, or other styling properties," for example,
expanding a thumbnail image in a product list view
into a full-bleed hero image in a product details view.
Now, you'll notice that use case doesn't mention the View
Transition API at all.
Instead, it describes a task that the developer
might want to implement or to accomplish,
where the View Transition API happens
to be the best choice to implement it with.
And this is really important because developers
don't generally prompt their coding agents
to use specific features.
They might not even know that those features exist.
Instead, they prompt their tools to implement use cases.
And so we need our guides to match the prompts
that developers are actually using.
So the second aspect of each of these guides
is that they're optimized for AI consumption.
And by that, I mean that each guide is concise,
it gets straight to the point, and it
contains only the minimum amount of information needed for the AI
to properly follow it.
This is more efficient than doing web search
because, even if the agent finds up-to-date and accurate
information on the web, which is not guaranteed,
it still has to read through all of that content,
use all of those tokens, just to find the bits that
are relevant to your use case.
Or perhaps not.
It might not find it.
Our guides are already scoped to the use case.
They're already vetted and tested for accuracy.
And they're already locally on your device.
So third, every guide, we include a section
that documents our specific recommendations and fallback
strategies to ensure that the implementation of the use case
works across browsers.
Now, I want to dig into that last part
because this cross-browser fallback guidance is,
in my opinion, the absolute best feature of this tool.
So let me explain how it works.
For each guide, we start by documenting
the ideal implementation using the most
modern solution available.
For this part of the guide, we do not take browser support
into consideration at all.
We assume that any feature can be used,
and we pick the best feature for the task at hand.
And we do this because we want to support people
who are experimenting with new features,
people who are building extensions, Electron apps,
building internal company tools, or really
any situation where cross-browser support is not
a major concern.
We don't want AI tools to prevent people
from using new APIs if their situation allows for it.
However, if any of the features in the ideal implementation
are not Baseline widely available,
then we always include a fallback recommendation.
And whenever possible, we make sure
that fallback recommendation works across browsers.
The only exception to this is things
like WebMCP, where there really is no cross-browser fallback.
But in all other cases, if there is a cross-browser fallback,
we use it.
And if there's not, we make it crystal clear
that the feature is only available in some browsers,
and we show how to properly feature detect for it.
And the reason we take this two-layered approach,
starting with the fully modern and then going
with the fallbacks, is so that the agent can pick and choose
how to implement the use case based on your site's browser
support requirements.
And that brings me to the final feature
I want to talk about in this package,
our Baseline integration.
I said that we want coding agents
to be able to customize their implementation based
on your browser support requirements.
And for this to work, two things need to happen.
First, you need to tell your agent what baseline
target or browsers you support.
Agents can sometimes guess or infer
this information from various config files in your project,
but we think it's better to be explicit,
and we recommend putting this information directly
into your AGENTS.md file.
If you don't declare any specific browser support
information, then the agent will assume
based on widely available.
Second, in the fallback section of each of our guides,
we include detailed browser compat data
so that the agent can then determine whether or not
it needs to use a particular fallback based on the browser
support requirements that you put in your AGENTS.md file.
For example, if you're building an Electron app
and you set in your AGENTS.md file
that you only need to support Chrome 144 or newer, then
if the agent encounters a fallback for something
like, say, scroll-driven animations-- which shipped
in Chrome 115-- then the agent can ignore that recommendation
and just stick with the modern implementation.
This allows the agent to custom tailor each guide's
implementation to the specific browser support
requirements of your project, rather
than always having to take a lowest common denominator
approach.
So that's a quick overview of Modern Web Guidance.
And I assume, at this point, many of you
are probably thinking, sounds great,
but how well does it actually work in practice?
So I do have some demos that I'm going to show,
so you will get to see it working.
But before I show those, I do want
to address this question directly because I
think it's an important one.
I think it's important that we, as an industry,
are able to evaluate the effectiveness of the skills
that we're using.
When we started this project, one of the main requirements
we had was to ensure that we had rigorous evals
for every single feature that we used.
As of now, our eval suite includes 554 distinct assertions
covering most of our guidance.
And we plan to expand that to full coverage
before our stable launch later this year.
And we run this full eval suite every single day
against many of the popular AI-coding models,
which right now includes Gemini 3.1, Claude Opus 4.7, and GPT
Here, on the screen, you can see a visualization
of the aggregate results of all of these evals
across all of these coding models.
The number in green on the right shows the average pass rate
of eval assertions for agents running with Modern Web

that we run against the agent's output.

indicator use case.
We run the prompt that you can see on the screen,
along with the following assertions
to test compliance with the guides.
For this use case, the test checks
to see that the implementation correctly
uses scroll-driven animations rather than relying
on scroll-event listeners.

for this particular run, with our guidance,
all the tests passed.
And without our guidance, all of them failed.
So this is a snapshot of how these models are performing
right now, but it's not hard to imagine
this changing in the future.
At some point, as the models improve
and as the browser landscape changes,
we fully expect that many of these evals
will start passing even without our guidance.
So I mentioned that we've run these evals daily.
Our plan here is to watch this closely, monitor the results,
and then remove use cases once we start
noticing that the unguided version is consistently
performing as well as the guided version in all
of the popular models.
This will allow us to keep the pack small, token efficient,
and focus just on the features that are new and not well known
by the models and not covered in the training.
But also keep in mind that new features
are shipping in browsers every single month,
and knowledge cutoffs continue to lag far behind.
So we believe this type of guidance
is going to continue to be necessary long into the future.
And speaking of the future, I now
want to talk a bit about how we see this project evolving
over time.
For this early preview, we're launching
with about a dozen high-level discipline
guides and more than 100 detailed use case guides,
but we're definitely not going to stop there.
Our plan is to continue adding more guides to give us
better coverage of the existing web platform,
but we're also going to be covering
new features as they land.
In fact, our goal with this tool is
to ensure that every single new web platform feature
that ships in Chrome is covered by this tool
by the time it lands in Chrome stable.
If you take a look at chromestatus.com,
you'll see that Chrome releases a lot of new features
every single milestone, so this is definitely an ambitious goal.
But it's one that we think is critical to support
the ongoing health and success of the web
in this new agentic world.
We're also currently engaging with other browser vendors
to try to get coverage for the features they're
shipping as well.
OK, so to recap what we've covered today-- first,
AI models have a knowledge gap and blind spots.
They recommend legacy solutions even when
there are newer and better alternatives.
Second, Modern Web Guidance fills those knowledge gaps
with vetted recommendations from Chrome experts.
This helps ensure coding agents have
a full and complete understanding of the modern web
platform, with clear instructions on how
to implement those features in a way that
is compatible across browsers.
And third, Chrome is committed to keeping Modern Web Guidance
up to date as the platform evolves
so that agentic coding will always
be at the forefront of modern web development,
rather than constantly lagging behind.
